posts.title: Race breakdown: Los Angeles Marathon (single image)
posts.caption:
Los Angeles Marathon is on Mar 7, 2027, and heat is the variable to watch: in 2026 it hit 82°F (27.8°C) by noon, and close to 1,000 runners stopped at mile 18.

The typical high is a mild 70°F (21.1°C), which is why a warm year catches people out. With 778 ft (237 m) of gain and 1,001 ft (305 m) of loss over 26.2 mi (42.195 km), the course itself is kind. A late-morning heat spike on legs that never trained warm is not. Race day is 16 weeks out.

When to start, counted back from Mar 7:

✅ Gut: race fuel in long runs starting between Dec 13 and Jan 10, race-level carbs by Jan 24 to Feb 7
✅ Pacing: goal-pace work in long runs from Dec 27
✅ Heat: for cover in a warm year, sessions Jan 24 to Feb 21, then 1 to 2 short sessions a week to race day
✅ Taper: the final 2 to 3 weeks, from Feb 14 or Feb 21

General guidelines, not a prescription. Heart condition, pregnancy or medication that affects heat tolerance? Talk to your doctor before heat sessions.

Full breakdown: raceproof.ai/races/los-angeles-marathon (link in bio).

SOURCES: Race numbers and 2026 weather: Raceproof's Los Angeles Marathon race page. Windows: Raceproof adaptation windows. Taper length: Raceproof coach consensus (coaching practice) and Smyth & Lawlor 2021.

posts.title: Research: Downhill repeats and squat strength (Martinez-Navarro et al. 2026, Sports)
posts.caption:
After a 3.1 mi (5 km) downhill run, trail runners who did weekly downhill repeats kept their squat strength (+4%). The rest lost 9.1%.

Martinez-Navarro and colleagues tested 36 experienced trail runners (25 men, 11 women) 4 to 6 weeks before a 65.9 mi (106 km) ultra-trail, with a 3.1 mi (5 km) treadmill descent at a 15% grade. The downhill-repeat group also had lower CK, a muscle damage marker (182 vs 290 U/L). Lower bounce and shorter steps on the way down were linked to keeping more strength.

Limits: an exploratory, observational study, so these are links, not proof. Only 21.6% of the runners did downhill repeats, the groups were small, and some did both downhill and strength work. The link between damage after the lab descent and after the race (r = 0.64, 27 finishers) fell to r = 0.429 without two extreme values.

Our take, not a finding of the study: train the descents your race has. Let long runs carry your race's descent per mile, add weekly descent by 10% or less, and make your last big downhill session 10 to 14 days out. That ramp and timing come from coaches, not studies. New to steep downhills? Start with relaxed downhills inside your long runs, and if soreness lasts more than about 3 days, wait for it to clear before the next one.

How often do you run downhill on purpose?

Save this for your next build.

SOURCES: Martinez-Navarro et al. 2026, Downhill Running-Induced Muscle Damage in Trail Runners: An Exploratory Study Regarding Training Background and Running Gait, Sports 14(1), doi.org/10.3390/sports14010012. Ramp: Raceproof adaptation rates (coaching practice: Uphill Athlete, Stewart via TrainingPeaks). Timing: Raceproof adaptation windows.

#raceproof #trailrunning #ultrarunning #downhillrunning #hillrunning
altText: Research, terrain, downhill. After a 3.1 mi (5 km) descent, trail runners who did weekly downhill repeats kept their squat strength. The rest lost 9.1%. Martinez-Navarro et al. 2026, Sports: Downhill Running-Induced Muscle Damage in Trail Runners.

What they found: squat strength after the descent, +4% with weekly downhill repeats vs minus 9.1% for the rest. CK, a muscle damage marker, 182 vs 290 U/L, lower with downhill repeats. 21.6% of the runners did weekly downhill repeats, so that group was small.

The key finding, bar chart of squat strength change after a 3.1 mi (5 km) treadmill descent: weekly downhill repeats +4%, no downhill repeats minus 9.1%. Average change, +4 plus or minus 10% vs minus 9.1 plus or minus 16.8%, d = 0.87. A link, not proof. Runners chose their own training, and some also lifted.

The study: 36 experienced trail runners, 25 men and 11 women, entered in a 65.9 mi (106 km) ultra-trail. Test: a 3.1 mi (5 km) treadmill descent at a 15% grade, 4 to 6 weeks before the race. Exploratory lab and field study. Observational, small groups.

What the study points to: 1, weekly downhill repeats were linked to legs that held up better on a long descent. 2, lower bounce and shorter steps on the way down were linked to keeping more strength. Summary from the Raceproof research library, not the authors' words.

Our take, not a finding of the study: train the descents your race has. Long runs carry your race's descent per mile. Add weekly descent by 10% or less. Last big downhill session 10 to 14 days out. Example card: Terrain, longest descent trained 3,500 ft (1,067 m), Building. Ramp and timing from coaches, not studies. New to steep downhills? Start with relaxed downhills inside long runs. posts.title: Myth vs proof: start everything as early as possible (Backup item, ultra Reel slot)
posts.caption:
Myth: start everything as early as possible.

Proof: each adaptation builds and fades at its own speed. Heat gains fade by about 2.5% for every day without heat, so a heat block months out is mostly gone by race day. In an older study, one downhill session protected the legs for up to about 6 weeks, and the effect was gone at 9. Climbing strength, on the other hand, lasts well.

When to start, counted back from race day:

✅ Heat: build 6 to 2 weeks out, then 1 to 2 short sessions a week to keep it
✅ Downhill: build from 12 to 8 weeks out, biggest weeks 5 to 3 weeks out, last big session 10 to 14 days before
✅ Gut: start 12 to 8 weeks out, race-level carbs by 4 to 6 weeks out, then race fuel in every long session
✅ Climbing: all block long

General guidelines, not a prescription. Heart condition, pregnancy or medication that affects heat tolerance? Talk to your doctor before heat sessions.

Share this with a training partner who starts everything in week 1.

SOURCES: Windows: Raceproof adaptation windows. Heat fade: Daanen et al. 2018, Sports Medicine. Downhill protection: Byrnes et al. 1985.
